genre/europese-kunstmuziek.text: Europe gave us the harmony of art music: major and minor, chords with fixed functions, melodies in regular phrases, and music that was written down. The colonists also brought hymns, marches, dances such as the waltz and the polka, and the song for voice and piano in the parlour. Sheet music and the piano made this music commonplace in nineteenth-century America too. Ragtime owes its notation, its form and its piano to European music, and Tin Pan Alley and the spirituals sung in several parts also built on it.
genre/europese-kunstmuziek.listen: Listen to An der schönen blauen Donau for the waltz in three beats and a melody that moves in regular phrases.

genre/europese-vrije-improvisatie.text: In the mid-1960s European musicians began to develop a free music of their own, one that leaned less on American swing and blues. In London the Spontaneous Music Ensemble of drummer John Stevens and the group AMM worked with small, attentive sounds. In Germany the pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach founded the Globe Unity Orchestra in 1966, and the saxophonist Peter Brötzmann of Wuppertal recorded the loud Machine Gun in 1968. In Amsterdam, Misha Mengelberg, Han Bennink and Willem Breuker started the Instant Composers Pool in 1967. Musicians set up labels of their own: ICP in Amsterdam, FMP in Berlin and Incus in London. The guitarist Derek Bailey spoke of non-idiomatic improvisation: free playing that is tied to no existing style at all.
genre/europese-vrije-improvisatie.listen: Don't look for a melody, but listen to the sound: how quickly do the players react to one another?

genre/fado.text: Fado arose in the first half of the nineteenth century in the poor harbour districts of Lisbon, such as Mouraria and Alfama. The word means fate. A singer, the fadista, sings of loss and longing, in Portuguese saudade, accompanied by a twelve-string Portuguese guitar and an ordinary guitar. Maria Severa became the first famous fadista around 1840. Amália Rodrigues made fado world-famous from the 1940s onwards. Since 2011 fado has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
genre/fado.listen: Listen to Barco Negro for the way the Portuguese guitar plays around the voice with clear, shimmering notes, and for the way Amália Rodrigues lets the long notes swell.

genre/fantasy-epos-en-wereldbouw.text: Around 2001, big fantasy series acquired musical worlds of their own. For the three Lord of the Rings films (2001–2003), Howard Shore wrote a network of leitmotifs for peoples, places and the Ring itself. The Shire sounds with Irish flute and fiddle, Mordor with heavy brass and a menacing choir. The choirs sing texts in the languages that Tolkien invented. Shore won Oscars for the first and the third film. John Williams gave Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (2001) an enchanting theme on the celesta that returns throughout the series. In How to Train Your Dragon (2010), John Powell used Scottish and Irish colours, such as bagpipes and fiddle. The principle behind this trend: music helps to build a credible world.
genre/fantasy-epos-en-wereldbouw.listen: Notice which instrument belongs to which place: hear how a folk instrument sketches a peaceful world and how choir and brass announce a threat.

genre/film-d-art-de-eerste-originele-fil.text: In 1908 the Parisian company Film d'Art wanted to make film respectable for a refined audience. It hired actors from the Comédie-Française and well-known writers. For L'assassinat du duc de Guise, Camille Saint-Saëns wrote a score for strings, piano and harmonium. It was one of the first times that a celebrated composer wrote music for one particular film. The music follows the action closely: a prelude and five tableaux, with moods of their own for the intrigue, the threat and the murder. Saint-Saëns later published the work as his Opus 128. The idea that a film deserves a score of its own, written to measure, begins here.
genre/film-d-art-de-eerste-originele-fil.listen: Listen to how the music changes character from tableau to tableau and follows the action step by step, without imitating separate sound effects.

genre/film-noir.text: Film noir is the name that French critics gave to dark American crime films of the 1940s. The music in them became harsher and more restless. Miklós Rózsa, a classically trained Hungarian, used sharp dissonances and a menacing march figure in Double Indemnity (1944). For Laura (1944), David Raksin wrote a single melancholy theme that he coloured differently each time. It later became a jazz standard. In Sunset Boulevard (1950), Franz Waxman combined leitmotifs with twisted dance music from Hollywood's past. The noir score lets go of the romance of the Golden Age and seeks tension in chromaticism, low brass and unexpected harmonies.
genre/film-noir.listen: Notice the dissonant chords and the low, threatening brass, and the melodies that stay restless instead of resolving.

genre/filmmusical.text: As soon as film could talk, it could sing too. From 1929 the studios turned out musicals at a high rate, often with songs by Broadway writers. In 42nd Street (1933), the choreographer Busby Berkeley turned rows of dancers into kaleidoscopic patterns for the camera. Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers danced to songs by Irving Berlin in Top Hat (1935). At MGM, the producer Arthur Freed built up a musical department of his own. Singin' in the Rain (1952) looks back with humour on the difficult transition to sound film. West Side Story (1961) brought Leonard Bernstein's Broadway musical to the screen, with jazz, Latin American rhythms and sharp dissonances. La La Land (2016), with music by Justin Hurwitz, pays explicit homage to this tradition.
genre/filmmusical.listen: Notice the moment when a spoken scene turns into song: often the orchestra is already creeping in under the dialogue before the singer begins.

genre/filmmuziek-uit-bollywood.text: In the Hindi films from Mumbai, Bollywood, songs are a fixed part of the story. The actors do not sing themselves: playback singers record the songs, and the actors lip-sync. Lata Mangeshkar and her sister Asha Bhosle sang thousands of film songs together. The music blends Indian classical and folk music with Western orchestras, jazz, rock and, later, disco and electronics.
genre/filmmuziek-uit-bollywood.listen: Listen to the high, clear voice of the playback singer above an orchestra in which Indian and Western instruments play together.

genre/flamenco.text: Flamenco grew up in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in Andalusia, above all among the gitanos, the Spanish Roma, in and around Seville, Jerez and Cádiz. In the cafés cantantes, which emerged from the middle of the nineteenth century, singing, guitar playing and dance became a stage art. The singing is raw and richly ornamented, with hand clapping and shouts as rhythmic accompaniment. Paco de Lucía and Camarón de la Isla renewed the genre from the 1970s onwards.
genre/flamenco.listen: Here La Niña de los Peines sings a soleá around 1910, one of the core forms of flamenco. Listen to how she stretches a single syllable over a whole series of notes, and how the guitar answers between her lines.

genre/folk-revival.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, young white musicians in Greenwich Village, New York, rediscovered old folk music: the folk revival. Dave Van Ronk made a new arrangement of House of the Rising Sun, which Bob Dylan put on his debut album in 1962. Dylan's protest songs later inspired Boudewijn de Groot as well.
genre/folk-revival.listen: Compare the descending bass line and the minor chords of Van Ronk and Dylan with the modal version from 1933.

genre/folkrock.text: In folk rock, folk melodies are played on electric guitars. In 1965 The Byrds in Los Angeles played Dylan's Mr. Tambourine Man on a twelve-string electric guitar, and Dylan himself went electric that same year. It belonged to the hippies of the late 1960s; Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young brought the folk rock of California, with three and four voices in close harmony. From 2009 Mumford & Sons brought back the banjo and acoustic guitar, and a few years later they were playing arenas with them.
genre/folkrock.listen: Listen to Our House for how closely the voices sit together: close harmony.

genre/franco-vlaamse-polyfonie.text: In the fifteenth century the best choral singers and composers in Europe came from northern France and the Low Countries, with the cathedral of Cambrai as an important breeding ground. Guillaume Dufay, Johannes Ockeghem and Josquin des Prez worked at courts and churches all over Europe. They wrote masses and motets for four or more equal voices that imitate one another. In 1436 Dufay wrote Nuper rosarum flores for the consecration of the cathedral of Florence.
genre/franco-vlaamse-polyfonie.listen: Listen to Dufay's motet for the cathedral of Florence for the way two low voices sing an old Gregorian melody in long notes while the higher voices move gracefully around it.

genre/frans-poetisch-realisme-en-les-six.text: In France, concert composers turned to film early on. Arthur Honegger wrote music in 1923 for La roue by Abel Gance. In the 1930s poetic realism emerged: sombre films about ordinary people, often with screenplays by Jacques Prévert. Maurice Jaubert wrote the music for L'Atalante (1934) and Le quai des brumes (1938). He believed that film music should not double the image, but add a poetic layer of its own to it. Georges Auric, a member of the composers' group Les Six, wrote the music for Jean Cocteau's La belle et la bête (1946). The sound is clear and light, with waltzes, chansons and small ensembles.
genre/frans-poetisch-realisme-en-les-six.listen: Notice the light, transparent instrumentation and the melodies that recall French chanson and the waltz.

genre/franse-barok.text: At the court of Louis XIV, music became an instrument of power. Jean-Baptiste Lully, born in Florence, became court composer in 1661, led a string orchestra known for its tight ensemble playing and, from 1673, wrote French operas full of dance. François Couperin refined harpsichord playing with small character pieces, and in Les Indes galantes (1735) Jean-Philippe Rameau put daring harmonies on the stage. Typically French were the dance rhythms and the rich ornamentation.
genre/franse-barok.listen: Listen to how Lully's march strides along solemnly and evenly, with a clear emphasis on the first beat.

genre/free-jazz.text: Free jazz let go of the conventions of theme, chord changes, time signature and tempo: musicians often improvise at the same time, and dissonances become material. The name comes from the album Free Jazz (1961) by Ornette Coleman, a Texan who came to New York from Los Angeles in late 1959 with a quartet without a piano.
genre/free-jazz.listen: Listen to Lonely Woman for the way the horns play the melody together, without piano and without fixed chord changes.

genre/french-house.text: In France, producers such as Daft Punk, Cassius and Étienne de Crécy made French house from the mid-1990s: house tracks with filters and samples from old disco and funk. In Around the World (1997) a single phrase is repeated over and over again while the accompaniment changes around the voice.
genre/french-house.listen: Listen to what changes in the accompaniment while the title keeps coming back.

genre/funk.text: Funk grew out of jazz, rhythm and blues and soul in the second half of the 1960s, with James Brown in the leading role. All the instruments come together on the first beat, 'on the one', and rhythm takes precedence over harmony: a song often stays on a single chord for minutes at a time. George Clinton with P-Funk, Stevie Wonder and Earth, Wind & Fire built on it.
genre/funk.listen: Listen to Sex Machine for the short, muted guitar stroke, the bass of Bootsy Collins and the call and response between Brown and Bobby Byrd.

genre/funkrock.text: In Cult of Personality (1988), Living Colour of New York mixed hard rock with funk; the guitarist Vernon Reid was part of the Black Rock Coalition. The Red Hot Chili Peppers of Los Angeles combined funk with punk and rock. It was a return to the roots: rock 'n' roll came from Black music.
genre/funkrock.listen: Listen to Give It Away for the way the bassist Flea slaps his strings and Anthony Kiedis raps more than he sings.

genre/fusion-en-jazzrock.text: Miles Davis listened to Jimi Hendrix, Sly and the Family Stone and James Brown, and played with electric instruments on In a Silent Way (1969) and, on Bitches Brew (1970), with several drummers at once. Fusion is the merging of jazz and rock, in which swing largely disappears. Steely Dan used jazz chords in pop songs, recorded with the best session musicians.
genre/fusion-en-jazzrock.listen: Listen to Birdland for the way the groove runs straight instead of swinging.

genre/g-funk.text: Dr. Dre, a former member of N.W.A., developed G-funk with The Chronic (1992): slow grooves with samples from George Clinton's P-Funk, a high synthesizer line and plenty of space. On California Love, Roger Troutman sings through a talk box. Later Dre chose a sparser sound: Still D.R.E. (1999) revolves around a minimal piano riff by Scott Storch.
genre/g-funk.listen: Listen to Nuthin' but a "G" Thang for the slow funk groove, the high synthesizer line and the relaxed flow of Snoop Dogg. Compare that with the silence around the piano riff in Still D.R.E.

genre/gabber-en-happy-hardcore.text: In the early 1990s gabber emerged in Rotterdam: hardcore at 160 to more than 200 bpm, with a distorted bass drum that sounds like a hammer. From 1992 the Thunderdome parties of ID&T drew thousands of visitors. Happy hardcore made the sound lighter, with cheerful melodies and high little voices, and scored hits in the Top 40.
genre/gabber-en-happy-hardcore.listen: Listen to Poing for the hard, distorted bass drum of early gabber, and to Wonderful Days (1994) for the fast tempo and cheerful melody of happy hardcore.

genre/gagaku.text: Gagaku is the court music of Japan, adopted from China and Korea and, since 701, supervised by a department of its own at the imperial court. It is regarded as the oldest living orchestral tradition in the world. The sho, a mouth organ with seventeen bamboo pipes, lays down floating chords, the hichiriki, a small double-reed oboe, plays the melody, and drums mark the slow tempo. The best-known piece is Etenraku, and since 2009 gagaku has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
genre/gagaku.listen: Listen to this choshi, a short free prelude, for the way the sho sounds slowly swelling chords before the other wind instruments join in.

genre/gamelan.text: A gamelan is an orchestra of bronze gongs, metallophones and drums from Java and Bali, played as a single instrument. Forerunners can already be seen on the reliefs of Borobudur, built around 800; in the Majapahit empire the instruments acquired their present form. Melodies run in cycles that are closed by a large gong, and each layer plays at its own tempo. The tunings slendro and pelog do not fit into the Western scale, which fascinated Debussy in 1889.
genre/gamelan.listen: This recording from 1971 has travelled since 1977 on the golden record of the Voyager. Listen to how the deep gong closes a cycle each time while higher instruments play around the melody.

genre/gangsta-rap.text: Gangsta rap took shape on the West Coast. After forerunners such as Schoolly D of Philadelphia and Ice-T of Los Angeles, N.W.A. of Compton, a suburb of Los Angeles, released Straight Outta Compton in 1988, with Fuck tha Police as an indictment of police violence. Lyrics about violence caused an outcry. In the mid-1990s the rivalry between the East and West Coast got out of hand; 2Pac (1996) and The Notorious B.I.G. (1997) were shot dead.
genre/gangsta-rap.listen: Listen to how directly and explicitly the lyrics accuse the Los Angeles police.

genre/garage.text: The Paradise Garage in New York, with the DJ Larry Levan, was one of the most important dance clubs from 1977 to 1987. When disco vanished from the charts, the music lived on there, with soulful vocals and gospel influences: garage, named after the club. In the 1990s UK garage emerged in England from this style.
genre/garage.listen: Listen to That's the Way Love Is for the soulful vocals and the piano chords above a house beat.

genre/garagerock.text: After the British Invasion, teenagers all over America started bands, rehearsed in the garage and recorded raw singles with a few chords, a screaming singer and a cheap organ. The Kingsmen already had a hit with Louie Louie in 1963, The Sonics of Tacoma played harder than anyone, and ? and the Mysterians scored with 96 Tears (1966). The compilation Nuggets (1972) brought these records to people's attention again, and punk built on them.
genre/garagerock.listen: Listen to Psycho for the distorted guitar, the singer's scream and the pounding drums: punk, ten years too early.

genre/garagerock-revival.text: In 2001 guitar rock suddenly sounded raw and short again. The Strokes of New York released Is This It, and The White Stripes, a duo from Detroit with only guitar and drums, released White Blood Cells. They harked back to the garage rock of the 1960s and to punk: few chords, a dry recording and no long solos. More bands with 'The' in their name followed, such as The Hives from Sweden and The Vines from Australia, and then the Yeah Yeah Yeahs.
genre/garagerock-revival.listen: Listen to Last Nite for the two guitars that interlock tightly, the dry drums and the voice of Julian Casablancas, which sounds as if he were singing through an old telephone.

genre/georgische-polyfonie.text: Around 1100 the Georgian scholar Ioane Petritsi already described three singing voices with names of their own: mzakhri, zhiri and bami. That centuries-old three-part singing is still alive in villages and churches. In eastern Kakheti, two richly ornamented solo voices float above a sustained bass, as in Chakrulo, which went into space in 1977 with the Voyager probes. In western Guria the highest voice, the krimanchuli, yodels above idiosyncratic countermelodies.
genre/georgische-polyfonie.listen: The men's choir Basiani sings Chakrulo, a Kakhetian song about preparing for a battle. Follow the two solo voices: how closely do they grate against each other, while the choir below holds a long bass note?

genre/giallo-en-italiaanse-horror.text: Giallo is the Italian word for yellow, after the yellow covers of cheap detective paperbacks. Around 1970 it became the name of a film genre: stylish murder thrillers. For Dario Argento's L'uccello dalle piume di cristallo (1970), Ennio Morricone wrote a mixture of lullabies, strange singing and atonal outbursts. For Profondo rosso (1975), Argento chose the Roman progressive rock band Goblin. Their music with synthesizer, organ, bass guitar and drums made the horror louder and more rhythmic. In Suspiria (1977), Goblin added celesta, whispering voices and a bouzouki. This approach later influenced John Carpenter and synth horror.
genre/giallo-en-italiaanse-horror.listen: Notice the contrast between a sweet, childlike motif and the hard, repeated riffs of band and synthesizer.

genre/glam-metal-en-stadionrock.text: After the launch of MTV in 1981, a rock band also had to look good. Glam metal combined hard rock with hairspray, make-up and tight trousers: pop songs in hard rock clothes, with choruses for stadiums. Bon Jovi and Van Halen scored big hits; in 1987 Guns N' Roses brought back the rawness.
genre/glam-metal-en-stadionrock.listen: Listen to Livin' on a Prayer for the guitar through a talk box and the key change in the final chorus.

genre/glamrock.text: Around 1972 rock acquired a theatrical side: costumes, make-up and a stage persona became just as important as the music. David Bowie invented Ziggy Stardust, a rock star from space, and became that character on stage and off it. The New Romantics of around 1980 leaned heavily on glam rock.
genre/glamrock.listen: Listen to how Bowie sings in Ziggy Stardust about a character rather than about himself.

genre/gnawa.text: The Gnawa of Morocco descend from people who were brought north as slaves from West Africa and the Sahel. In nocturnal rituals, the lila, a master, the maâlem, leads the music on the guembri, a three-string bass lute with a soundbox covered in camel skin. Around it the qraqeb, metal castanets, rattle, and a choir sings in call and response until the participants fall into a trance. Since 2019 gnawa has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
genre/gnawa.listen: Listen to how Mahmoud Guinia's deep guembri keeps repeating a short pattern while the qraqeb set a fast, rattling rhythm against it.

genre/golden-age-hiphop.text: In the late 1980s samplers became affordable and producers built beats from pieces of existing recordings: the golden age of hip hop. Public Enemy piled up samples, sirens and scratches, De La Soul chose a playful tone, and the Wu-Tang Clan used lo-fi beats with samples from kung fu films. After a lawsuit against Biz Markie in 1991, it became customary to ask permission for every sample and to pay for it.
genre/golden-age-hiphop.listen: Listen to Night of the Living Baseheads for the way The Bomb Squad stacks layer upon layer: samples, sirens, scratches and speeches.

genre/golden-age-symfonisch-hollywood-en.text: With King Kong (1933), Max Steiner showed what a continuous orchestral score could do in a sound film. The Hollywood studios had orchestras and music departments of their own. European composers such as Steiner and Erich Wolfgang Korngold from Vienna and Franz Waxman from Germany brought with them the language of Wagner, Richard Strauss and operetta. Typical features are the large symphony orchestra, lush strings, brass fanfares and the leitmotif: every character or idea gets a theme of its own that returns and changes. The music often follows the action beat for beat, which is called ‘Mickey Mousing’. Gone with the Wind (1939) and Casablanca (1942) became the model for the classic Hollywood score.
genre/golden-age-symfonisch-hollywood-en.listen: Follow one theme and hear how it returns in a different instrumentation or key when the story changes.

genre/gothic-rock.text: Gothic rock grew out of post-punk: dark, echoing and slow. In 1979 Bauhaus of Northampton recorded Bela Lugosi's Dead, nine minutes long, named after the actor who played Dracula. The Cure appear with A Forest on the album Seventeen Seconds (1980). The black clothes and dark hair of the singer Robert Smith became the uniform of a new youth culture, the goths.
genre/gothic-rock.listen: In A Forest, listen for the guitar with a chorus effect and the bass that keeps repeating the same motif.

genre/gouden-eeuw-van-de-hindi-filmmuzie.text: The first Indian sound film, Alam Ara (1931), already had songs, and singing remained the core of the Hindi film. Actors usually do not sing themselves. Playback singers such as Lata Mangeshkar, Mohammed Rafi and Mukesh record the songs, and the actors lip-sync. In the 1940s and 1950s, composers such as Naushad, S.D. Burman and the duo Shankar-Jaikishan became leading figures. They combined ragas and Indian instruments such as sitar, tabla and shehnai with Western strings, mandolin and accordion. Raj Kapoor's Awaara (1951) even became a hit in the Soviet Union. Mughal-e-Azam (1960) brought classical Indian singing and a large orchestra together.
genre/gouden-eeuw-van-de-hindi-filmmuzie.listen: Notice the blend of Indian melodies and rhythms with Western strings, and the clear, ornamented vocal line.

genre/gregoriaans.text: Around 750 the Frankish kings Pepin and Charlemagne wanted singing throughout their realm to be done as in Rome. In Metz, where Bishop Chrodegang had singers trained, Roman chant fused with the local Gallican chant; the result later took its name from Pope Gregory the Great. To remember the melodies, neumes appeared, little signs above the text. Around 1025 Guido of Arezzo added the staff.
genre/gregoriaans.listen: Listen to how the monks sing in unison, without a beat and without accompaniment, and to how the melody follows the text: sometimes one note per syllable, sometimes a long flourish on a single vowel.

genre/grime.text: In the early 2000s grime emerged in East London: rap in a London accent over fast, bare, electronic beats at around 140 bpm, with influences from UK garage, jungle and dancehall. MCs battled one another on pirate radio. In 2003 Dizzee Rascal won the Mercury Prize with his debut Boy in da Corner, and later Skepta and Stormzy became big stars.
genre/grime.listen: Listen to I Luv U for the cold, abrasive synthesizers and the fast, nervous flow of Dizzee Rascal.

genre/griots-en-de-kora.text: In the Mali Empire, which Sundiata Keita founded around 1235, the jeli or griots became the memory of society. These hereditary families of singers and musicians know genealogies and heroic tales by heart and pass them on orally, accompanied by the balafon, the ngoni lute and the kora, a harp with 21 strings. The balafon that, according to tradition, already belonged to Sundiata is still kept by the Kouyaté family in Niagassola.
genre/griots-en-de-kora.listen: Foday Musa Suso, a griot from Gambia, sings and plays the story of Sunjata, the founder of the Mali Empire. Listen to how the kora repeats and varies a short pattern while the voice above it tells the tale.

genre/grunge.text: In the late 1980s, around the small label Sub Pop in Seattle, a scene emerged that mixed punk and heavy metal into a raw, heavy sound. In January 1992 Nirvana's Nevermind knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous off the top of the American album chart. Pearl Jam and Soundgarden also came from Seattle.
genre/grunge.listen: In Smells Like Teen Spirit, listen for the quiet-loud dynamics: soft verses and loud choruses on four power chords.

genre/gypsy-jazz-jazz-manouche.text: In 1934 the guitarist Django Reinhardt and the violinist Stéphane Grappelli founded the Quintette du Hot Club de France in Paris. It was a jazz band without horns or drums: solo guitar, violin, two rhythm guitars and double bass. The rhythm guitars play la pompe, a short, dry chord on every beat that replaces the drums. Reinhardt came from a family of Manouches, travelling Sinti, and after a fire in 1928 had been left almost unable to use two fingers of his left hand; he developed a technique of his own. The quintet is regarded as the first European jazz group with a sound of its own. Nuages became a big hit in 1940, in occupied Paris. The music lives on in Sinti communities in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where the Rosenberg Trio from Brabant became internationally known.
genre/gypsy-jazz-jazz-manouche.listen: Listen to how the rhythm guitars take over the role of the drummer.

genre/habanera.text: The habanera is a Cuban dance of the nineteenth century, named after Havana. Its characteristic feature is a rhythm in 2/4 with a dotted first beat and an accent that falls just off the beat. Via Spain and via the ports of the Caribbean, that rhythm spread throughout the Americas: in New Orleans you can hear it in early jazz, and it also underlies the Afro-Cuban music of Latin jazz.
genre/habanera.listen: Listen to La Paloma for the swaying habanera rhythm in the accompaniment: long, short and then two equal beats.

genre/hammer-horror-en-britse-genrefilm.text: From the mid-1950s the British studio Hammer made colourful horror films at Bray Studios. The musical director John Hollingsworth often commissioned modern concert composers. James Bernard became the regular voice of Hammer. For Dracula (1958) he based the main motif on three notes that follow the rhythm of the name Dracula. His music is loud and direct, with brass, timpani and dissonant strings. Tristram Cary, a pioneer of electronic music, wrote Quatermass and the Pit (1967). Elisabeth Lutyens, one of the first British twelve-tone composers, worked on the studio's psychological thrillers, such as Paranoiac (1963).
genre/hammer-horror-en-britse-genrefilm.listen: Listen to how the three-note Dracula motif keeps returning in brass and timpani and clashes with dissonant strings.

genre/hard-bop.text: On the East Coast, many Black musicians found Cool Jazz too restrained. Hard bop uses the harmony and solo technique of bebop, but mixes them with rhythm and blues, gospel and blues, with a heavier groove. Much of it appeared on the New York label Blue Note, such as John Coltrane's Blue Train (1957).
genre/hard-bop.listen: In Blue Train, listen for the heavy groove and the bluesy theme that the horns play together.

genre/hardcore-punk.text: Around 1980 American bands made punk shorter, faster and harder: hardcore. Black Flag from Los Angeles, and Minor Threat and Bad Brains from Washington, played songs of less than two minutes in small venues. They released their records themselves, on labels such as SST and Dischord, and organised their own tours: do it yourself. Grunge and emo later emerged from that scene.
genre/hardcore-punk.listen: Listen to Straight Edge for the furious tempo, the short song and the lyrics, which are shouted rather than sung.

genre/hardrock-en-heavy-metal.text: Hard rock came out of the blues rock of Cream, Jimi Hendrix and The Yardbirds. Led Zeppelin was formed in London in 1968, and Deep Purple and Black Sabbath laid the foundations for heavy metal. The guitar sounds distorted: what was a fault to a technician became a choice of sound for guitarists.
genre/hardrock-en-heavy-metal.listen: Play along with the riff of Smoke on the Water: fourths on G, B-flat and C, the first thing beginner guitarists learn.

genre/hardstyle.text: Around 2000 hardstyle emerged in the Netherlands, out of German hard trance and Dutch hardcore. The organisation Q-dance held parties such as Qlubtempo and Qlimax, had the name hardstyle registered in 2002 and launched the festival Defqon.1 in 2003. The basis is a hard, distorted bass drum, at first around 140 to 150 bpm and later faster. Between the kicks falls a reverse bass: a bass note that sounds exactly between the bass drums. Above it come big synthesizer melodies. Headhunterz, Showtek and Brennan Heart became the best-known names.
genre/hardstyle.listen: Listen to Just Begun for the way the bass keeps falling in between the hard bass drums: the reverse bass that makes hardstyle recognisable.

genre/harlem-renaissance.text: In the 1920s Harlem, a neighbourhood in the north of Manhattan, became the cultural centre of Black America. Writers such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston, visual artists and musicians together shaped what later came to be called the Harlem Renaissance. The musical Shuffle Along by Noble Sissle and Eubie Blake was a success on Broadway in 1921, with an all-Black cast. At the Cotton Club, Black performers played for an exclusively white audience; Duke Ellington led the house orchestra there from 1927 to 1931 and became known across the country through radio broadcasts, followed by Cab Calloway. At the Savoy Ballroom, opened in 1926, Black and white audiences did dance together. Music, dance and literature expressed a new self-confidence.
genre/harlem-renaissance.listen: Listen to the singing and the tone colours of the orchestra: this was music for theatre, revue and radio.

genre/hawaiaanse-slack-key-en-steelgitaa.text: Around 1832 King Kamehameha III brought Mexican vaqueros to Hawaii to teach the population how to work with cattle, and according to many historians the guitar came with them. Hawaiians tuned the strings down to an open chord: slack key, or kī hōʻalu. In the 1880s Joseph Kekuku slid a metal bar over the strings, the beginning of the steel guitar. From the 1910s that sound conquered America and later coloured country music.
genre/hawaiaanse-slack-key-en-steelgitaa.listen: Gabby Pahinui, the great name of slack key, sings and plays Hiʻilawe. Listen to the guitar: can you hear how the low strings keep running like a bass while he plays the melody above?

genre/heartland-rock.text: Bruce Springsteen of New Jersey made rock about ordinary people, work, cars and the dream of getting away. For Born to Run (1975) he built a wall of sound modelled on Phil Spector's Wall of Sound. Born in the U.S.A. (1984) sounds like an anthem, but is about a Vietnam veteran who cannot find work.
genre/heartland-rock.listen: In Born to Run, try to tell the layers apart: guitars, piano, organ, saxophone and glockenspiel.

genre/heilig-minimalisme.text: In Soviet-era Estonia, Arvo Pärt found a sober style in 1976 that he called tintinnabuli, after the Latin word for little bells. A melody wanders slowly around while a second voice plays only the notes of a single triad. In Cantus (1977), scales descend above a tolling bell. The Pole Henryk Górecki wrote his Third Symphony in 1976; a recording from 1992 sold more than a million copies.
genre/heilig-minimalisme.listen: Listen to how in Cantus the strings play slowly descending scales, ever slower in the lower voices, while a bell keeps tolling.

genre/het-nederlandstalige-lied.text: In the 1990s the Dutch-language song grew for a large audience: from 1994 Marco Borsato had one hit after another with ballads. Acda en de Munnik continued the line of kleinkunst, and BLØF, with Geike Arnaert, made Zoutelande (2017), one of the biggest hits ever in the Netherlands. Around 2020 Snelle and Froukje found their audience through TikTok and YouTube.
genre/het-nederlandstalige-lied.listen: Listen to Zoutelande for a quiet duet about a beach in Zeeland.

genre/het-nieuwe-pianotrio.text: The piano trio of piano, double bass and drums is a classic jazz line-up. Around 1960, the trio of Bill Evans with the bassist Scott LaFaro and the drummer Paul Motian showed that the three players can play together as equals, instead of bass and drums merely accompanying. From the 1990s a new generation gave the trio a sound of its own. Brad Mehldau played songs by Radiohead and Nick Drake. The Swedish Esbjörn Svensson Trio, e.s.t. for short, used effects and electronics, played in rock venues and in 2006 became the first European jazz group on the cover of the American magazine DownBeat. The Bad Plus played Nirvana. The Armenian pianist Tigran Hamasyan combines folk music from his country with complex rhythms from metal. Svensson died in a diving accident in 2008.
genre/het-nieuwe-pianotrio.listen: Notice how bass and drums do not merely accompany, but join the conversation with the piano.

genre/highlife.text: Highlife grew up in Ghana in the first half of the twentieth century out of West African rhythms, church hymns and the music of military bands and sailors. In the 1950s the trumpeter E.T. Mensah, the King of Highlife, turned it into dance-band music with horns and jazz influences. Alongside it existed guitar-band highlife, with several guitars interweaving short patterns. Out of highlife and jazz, Afrobeat later emerged in Nigeria.
genre/highlife.listen: Listen to Queen's Visit for the horns and the guitars that interweave short, repeated patterns above a light, danceable groove.

genre/himene-tarava.text: After English missionaries arrived in Tahiti in 1797, many dances were suppressed, but singing in a choir remained permitted. Tahitians fused their own part-singing with the Protestant hymns, and himene accordingly comes from the English hymn. A lead singer begins, and the others join in one by one. Men sing deep, rhythmic sounds, women high lines. Since 1881 choirs have competed at the festivities around 14 July.
genre/himene-tarava.listen: This himene tārava was recorded on 5 March 1979 at Point Venus, where the missionaries once landed. Listen to the lowest layer: can you hear the men giving the rhythm with short, deep thrusts beneath the high women's voices?

genre/historisch-epos-en-sandalenfilm.text: In the 1950s Hollywood fought television with widescreen, colour and long historical films. The music grew along with them. For Quo Vadis (1951), Miklós Rózsa researched ancient Greek and Roman melodies, and for Ben-Hur (1959) he wrote more than two hours of music, with fanfares, marches and chorales. Alex North gave Spartacus (1960) a harder, more modern sound with dissonances and unusual tone colours. In Lawrence of Arabia (1962), Maurice Jarre used an ondes Martenot and a great deal of percussion to evoke the desert. Typical features are an overture and intermission music, as in opera, and a large orchestra with a lot of brass.
genre/historisch-epos-en-sandalenfilm.listen: Notice the brass and percussion, and how the overture presents the main themes of the film one after another.

genre/hollywoodwestern.text: After the war the Hollywood Western acquired a musical identity of its own. In High Noon (1952), Dimitri Tiomkin, a Russian émigré, had a ballad return again and again, sung by Tex Ritter. The song became a hit and won an Oscar, and after that many Westerns got a title song. For The Big Country (1958), Jerome Moross wrote a broad theme with bouncing rhythms and the open sound of Copland. In The Magnificent Seven (1960), Elmer Bernstein set down a syncopated main theme with a Mexican flavour, which later became familiar from cigarette commercials. Typical features are galloping rhythms, brass fanfares, guitar and melodies that recall folk songs.
genre/hollywoodwestern.listen: Notice the rhythm that imitates a galloping horse and the broad melody in horns and strings above it.

genre/horror-synth-carpenter-school.text: John Carpenter directed his films himself and also wrote the music, partly because there was no money for a composer. For Assault on Precinct 13 (1976) and Halloween (1978) he used synthesizers and piano. The Halloween theme is in an unusual 5/4 time; Carpenter learned that time signature from his father, a music teacher. Simple ostinatos, low drones and sharp synthesizer stabs create the tension. From Escape from New York (1981) he worked with the sound designer Alan Howarth. Charles Bernstein followed the style in A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984). In Italy the band Goblin was an important forerunner of this sound.
genre/horror-synth-carpenter-school.listen: Notice the 5/4 time and the simple, endlessly repeated piano figure above a low synthesizer note.

genre/house.text: From 1977 Frankie Knuckles played a mix of disco, soul and European synth-pop at The Warehouse in Chicago, for a mainly Black and gay crowd. From 1984 young producers in Chicago began making tracks themselves with a drum machine, a synthesizer and a tape recorder. At its core, house is disco with a machine: four-on-the-floor at around 120 bpm.
genre/house.listen: Listen to Your Love for the bass drum on every beat beneath a synthesizer line that keeps coming back.

genre/hyperpop.text: Hyperpop exaggerates everything about pop: high, distorted voices with Auto-Tune, bright synthesizers, hard bass and sudden twists. Its roots lie with the London label PC Music of A. G. Cook and with the producer SOPHIE, from 2013. The name came into use in 2019 via a Spotify playlist, with 100 gecs as a well-known act, and in 2024 Charli XCX brought the style to a wide audience with Brat.
genre/hyperpop.listen: Listen to Immaterial for the metallic synthesizers, the high voices and the cheerful exaggeration.

genre/idm.text: IDM, intelligent dance music, is electronic music to listen to rather than dance to. In 1992 the Sheffield label Warp released the compilation Artificial Intelligence, and Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada made music with complicated rhythms, unusual sounds and ambient-like melodies.
genre/idm.listen: Listen to Xtal for the soft chords and a wordless voice above a simple beat.

genre/ierse-traditionele-muziek.text: Around 1700 the blind harpist Turlough O'Carolan travelled from one Irish noble family to another and wrote melodies for them. When the last of the old harpers gathered in Belfast in 1792, Edward Bunting wrote down their music. After that, dance music gained the upper hand: reels, jigs and hornpipes on fiddle, flute and uilleann pipes, a bagpipe that you fill with a bellows under the elbow. In the session, an informal gathering in the pub, this centuries-old music lives on.
genre/ierse-traditionele-muziek.listen: The Bothy Band plays a set of jigs, beginning with The Kesh. Count along: can you hear that every beat divides into three? Also notice the hoarse sound of the uilleann pipes between fiddle and flute.

genre/impressionisme.text: In Paris, Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel searched for music that sounds like light, water and clouds. Debussy's Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894) begins with a free, floating flute melody. At the world fair of 1889, Debussy heard a Javanese gamelan orchestra, and in Pagodes (1903) that echoes in pentatonic melodies and gong-like basses. Chords no longer had to resolve, but were allowed simply to sound as colour.
genre/impressionisme.listen: Listen to how the flute in the Prélude seems to wander without a fixed beat, and how harp and horns lay colour around it.

genre/indiase-klassieke-muziek.text: The classical music of North India is built on the raga, a scale with fixed melodic turns and a character of its own, and the tala, a rhythmic cycle. A performance often begins slowly and freely, above a sustained fundamental note, the drone, and then speeds up together with the tabla. In the 1960s the sitar player Ravi Shankar brought this music to the West: he taught George Harrison and played at the festivals of Monterey (1967) and Woodstock (1969).
genre/indiase-klassieke-muziek.listen: In the alap of Raga Malkauns, listen to how the sitar begins freely and without a fixed beat above the sustained drone: the raga is built up note by note.

genre/indiefolk.text: Around 2008 young musicians brought back acoustic folk, with the approach of indie rock: recording and releasing it themselves on small record labels. On their 2008 debut, Fleet Foxes of Seattle sang in several parts like a choir. Bon Iver recorded his first album in a hunting cabin in Wisconsin, and Mumford & Sons of London made the banjo and the mandolin popular at big festivals. The songs often begin softly and grow into an exuberant ending.
genre/indiefolk.listen: In White Winter Hymnal, listen to how the voices come in with the same line one after another, like a canon, while the drums grow steadily fuller.

genre/indiepop-en-shoegaze.text: From the late 1970s small British labels such as Rough Trade and Creation released guitar music outside the big record companies: indie, short for independent. In 1986 the music paper NME put together a cassette of young bands, C86, which gave its name to the sweet indie pop. Around 1990 shoegaze emerged: bands such as My Bloody Valentine and Slowdive built walls of distorted, floating guitars, and on stage looked mostly at their effects pedals, at their shoes.
genre/indiepop-en-shoegaze.listen: Listen to Only Shallow for the way the guitars become one undulating cloud of sound, with the vocals half hidden in it.

genre/indopop.text: Alongside the fast indorock, Indo musicians in the Netherlands also made gentle, melodic pop, with two-part singing in the style of the Everly Brothers. The brothers Riem and Ruud de Wolff, The Blue Diamonds, had a number one hit in Germany and the Netherlands in 1960 with Ramona. Anneke Grönloh, born in Indonesia, scored in 1962 with Brandend zand.
genre/indopop.listen: Listen to Ramona for the two-part singing and the quiet guitar accompaniment.

genre/indorock.text: After 1949, Indo-Dutch people brought krontjong and the Hawaiian guitar with them; with American country and rock 'n' roll, this fused in the Netherlands into indorock. It is fast, often instrumental guitar music with a lot of echo and a wild show. The Tielman Brothers played in German clubs from 1959, a year before the Beatles came to Hamburg in 1960.
genre/indorock.listen: Listen to Rock Little Baby of Mine for the way an echo unit makes every fast guitar note reverberate.

genre/industrial.text: In the late 1970s Throbbing Gristle of London made music from noise, tape loops and electronics, released on their own label Industrial Records: industrial. Cabaret Voltaire of Sheffield worked in the same way. From 1980 Einstürzende Neubauten of Berlin hit metal plates and used power drills as instruments. In the late 1980s Nine Inch Nails, with Pretty Hate Machine (1989) and The Downward Spiral (1994), brought industrial to rock and the charts.
genre/industrial.listen: Listen to Mr. Self Destruct, the opening track of The Downward Spiral, for the mechanical beat, the distorted sounds and the voice of Trent Reznor going from whispering to screaming.

genre/industrial-en-elektronische-textuu.text: Trent Reznor, founder of the industrial band Nine Inch Nails, and Atticus Ross began their collaboration with the director David Fincher in 2010 on The Social Network, for which they won an Oscar. They work with distorted synthesizers, piano, noise and sounds that are almost like sound design. After The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011) and Gone Girl (2014), they made the music for the Pixar film Soul (2020) with the jazz musician Jon Batiste. For Challengers (2024) they wrote driving techno. In 2010 the French duo Daft Punk gave Tron: Legacy a mixture of orchestra and electronics. In this way the difference between film score and electronic record becomes blurred.
genre/industrial-en-elektronische-textuu.listen: Notice how noise, distortion and a simple piano motif together create tension, and the dance beat in Challengers.

genre/inheemse-muziek-van-noord-amerika.text: Among the Indigenous peoples of North America, music is centuries old and interwoven with prayer, healing, hunting and dance. On the Great Plains, a group of singers sits in a circle around one large drum; the lead singer begins a song and the others take it up. In the late nineteenth century, when the American government was taking land and banning ceremonies, the powwow grew out of the Grass Dance and other traditions, a gathering where peoples sing and dance together.
genre/inheemse-muziek-van-noord-amerika.listen: In this Grass Dance song, listen to how the lead singer begins the first line alone, how the group repeats it and how the drum carries on in a tight, even beat.

genre/isicathamiya-en-zuid-afrikaanse-ko.text: After the First World War, Zulu men moved from the countryside of Natal to the mines and factories, where they lived in men's hostels. There a cappella choirs emerged that competed against one another, with soft, creeping dance steps; isicathamiya comes from a Zulu word for walking carefully, like a cat. In 1939 Solomon Linda and his Evening Birds recorded Mbube, the source of The Lion Sleeps Tonight. Ladysmith Black Mambazo later took the style all over the world, partly through Paul Simon's Graceland.
genre/isicathamiya-en-zuid-afrikaanse-ko.listen: Listen to Mbube for how the low voices keep repeating the same pattern while Solomon Linda improvises high above it. That melody later became The Lion Sleeps Tonight.

genre/italiaans-neorealisme.text: After the Second World War, Italian directors filmed in the street, with non-professional actors and little money. Roberto Rossellini made Roma città aperta (1945), with music by his brother Renzo Rossellini. Vittorio De Sica often worked with Alessandro Cicognini, on films including Sciuscià (1946), Ladri di biciclette (1948) and Umberto D. (1952). Remarkably, the music is not always sober. Cicognini wrote melodious, sentimental themes that underline the characters' sorrow. Set against this are silent scenes with only street sounds. Neorealism brought film into everyday life. The Italian film music that followed built on those simple, singing melodies.
genre/italiaans-neorealisme.listen: Notice the simple, singing theme and how the orchestra magnifies the emotion of a small, everyday scene.

genre/italiaanse-auteursfilm-fellini-vis.text: In the 1950s Federico Fellini and Luchino Visconti grew out of neorealism into a personal, poetic film style. Their most important musical partner was Nino Rota, who studied in Milan and Rome and also wrote operas and concert works. Rota worked with Fellini from Lo sceicco bianco (1952) to Prova d'orchestra (1979). His music borrows from the circus, the brass band, the music hall and the waltz, and often sounds cheerful and wistful at the same time. In La strada (1954), Gelsomina plays the main theme on her trumpet. For 8½ (1963) he wrote a circus march that closes the film. For Visconti's Il Gattopardo (1963) he adapted, among other things, an unknown waltz by Verdi.
genre/italiaanse-auteursfilm-fellini-vis.listen: Notice the blend of circus march and melancholy: the same melody sounds festive and sad at once.

genre/italo-disco.text: In Italy a form of electronic dance music of its own emerged, a mixture of synth-pop and Eurodisco, with Giorgio Moroder as the great forerunner. Producers released solo projects under invented names, with English lyrics in an Italian accent. Arpeggiators and vocoders define the sound.
genre/italo-disco.listen: Listen to Dolce Vita for the bass in eighth notes from an arpeggiator, like an engine that never stops.

genre/j-pop.text: In the late 1980s the term J-pop came into use in Japan for modern Japanese pop music, as distinct from the older, schlager-like kayōkyoku. In the 1990s producers and female singers became stars, and with the album First Love (1999), with R&B influences, Hikaru Utada made the best-selling Japanese record ever. J-pop is closely connected with anime, games and idol groups.
genre/j-pop.listen: Listen to Automatic for how R&B rhythms and a soft voice go together with a Japanese text.

genre/japanse-gouden-eeuw-en-tokusatsu.text: In the 1950s Japanese film drew worldwide attention. Fumio Hayasaka, Akira Kurosawa's regular composer, wrote a bolero modelled on Ravel for Rashōmon (1950) and mixed Japanese and Western sounds in Shichinin no samurai (1954). After his death in 1955, his pupil Masaru Sato took over the work for Kurosawa. For Yōjimbō (1961), Sato wrote a rough, almost comical theme. Akira Ifukube gave Gojira (1954) a heavy, repeated march motif. He also made the monster's roar, using a double bass. In this way tokusatsu, the Japanese special-effects film, acquired a musical voice of its own.
genre/japanse-gouden-eeuw-en-tokusatsu.listen: Notice the repeated, heavy ostinato in Ifukube and the way Japanese and Western sounds alternate.

genre/japanse-jazz.text: Jazz was already heard in Japan in the 1920s, in the dance halls of Osaka and Kobe. During the Second World War it was regarded as the music of the enemy. After 1945 Japanese musicians played in clubs for the American occupation soldiers and in this way learned swing and bebop. Typically Japanese is the jazz kissa: a café where you listen quietly to records on a good sound system. The pianist Toshiko Akiyoshi left for Berklee in Boston in 1956; the saxophonist Sadao Watanabe followed in 1962 and brought bossa nova and new theory back with him on his return. In the 1970s the label Three Blind Mice recorded Japanese trios with great care for the sound. Yosuke Yamashita played free jazz, Terumasa Hino later fusion as well. After 2000 the pianist Hiromi became known all over the world.
genre/japanse-jazz.listen: Listen to the piano trios: clearly recorded, with close attention to every note.

genre/japanse-nieuwe-golf-en-arthouse.text: Around 1960 Japanese directors such as Nagisa Ōshima, Masaki Kobayashi and Hiroshi Teshigahara made radical, modern films. Tōru Takemitsu, a largely self-taught composer, wrote the music for many of them. In Seppuku (1962) he used the biwa, a Japanese lute, with sharp, isolated notes. For Suna no onna (1964) he processed string sounds into a dry, grainy sound. He saw sound and silence as a single whole. Ryuichi Sakamoto, a member of Yellow Magic Orchestra, acted in Ōshima's Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence (1983) and wrote the music for it. Takemitsu worked with Kurosawa on Ran (1985).
genre/japanse-nieuwe-golf-en-arthouse.listen: Notice silence as part of the music, and isolated, sharp sounds instead of continuous melodies.

genre/jazz-in-film.text: For a long time jazz in Hollywood sounded only as source music, for instance from a band in a nightclub. Alex North changed that with A Streetcar Named Desire (1951). He used jazz in the score itself, to convey the sensuality and tension of New Orleans. For The Man with the Golden Arm (1955), about an addicted drummer, Elmer Bernstein wrote a hard-driving big band score. Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn made the music for Anatomy of a Murder (1959), and Ellington plays a small role in the film himself. In France, Miles Davis improvised the music for Ascenseur pour l'échafaud. In this way jazz became the sound of the city, the night and modern man.
genre/jazz-in-film.listen: Notice the horns, the swing and the blue notes, and how the rhythm of jazz heightens the tension of a scene.

genre/jazz-in-nederland.text: In 1926 Theo Uden Masman founded The Ramblers, the best-known Dutch dance orchestra of the pre-war years. In 1935 and 1937 it made records with the American saxophonist Coleman Hawkins, who was living in Europe at the time. After the Liberation, the Dutch Swing College Band, founded in 1945, played traditional jazz. In the 1950s the singer Rita Reys became internationally known as 'Europe's First Lady of Jazz', later often with the pianist Pim Jacobs. In the 1960s an avant-garde of its own emerged around Misha Mengelberg, Han Bennink and Willem Breuker, with the Instant Composers Pool (1967) and the Amsterdam Bimhuis (1974). From 1976 Paul Acket organised the North Sea Jazz Festival in The Hague, which has been held in Rotterdam since 2006. Later came Candy Dulfer, the New Cool Collective of Benjamin Herman and the guitarist Reinier Baas, among others.
genre/jazz-in-nederland.listen: Compare the different Dutch sounds: dance orchestra, Dixieland and modern.

genre/jazzfunk.text: Jazz-funk emphasises the groove of funk musicians such as James Brown and Sly Stone. The rhythm section plays short, repeated patterns that interlock; the horns and keyboards play short, rhythmic lines over them. Synthesizers gained a permanent place. In 1973 Herbie Hancock recorded Head Hunters, which for a long time was the best-selling jazz album; he plays the bass line of Chameleon himself on a synthesizer. The trumpeter Donald Byrd worked with the producers Larry and Fonce Mizell and made soul and funk records for Blue Note. The vibraphonist Roy Ayers and the keyboardist Lonnie Liston Smith also won a large audience. In the 1980s British DJs collected these records as rare groove, and in hip hop they were sampled extensively.
genre/jazzfunk.listen: Find the smallest repeated pattern in the bass and listen to how the other instruments hook into it.

genre/jazzrap.text: From the very beginning, hip hop producers used samples: short pieces of existing records that are repeated as the basis for a track. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, groups in New York began deliberately sampling jazz records. A Tribe Called Quest built The Low End Theory (1991) on jazz samples and had the bassist Ron Carter play on it. Gang Starr, with the rapper Guru and the producer DJ Premier, made Jazz Thing in 1990 for the film Mo' Better Blues. In 1993 Guru recorded Jazzmatazz, with jazz musicians such as Donald Byrd and Roy Ayers in the studio. The British group Us3 gained access to the Blue Note archive and scored with Cantaloop, built on Herbie Hancock's Cantaloupe Island. In this way a new generation got to know jazz through hip hop.
genre/jazzrap.listen: Find the sample: which piece of jazz is repeated over and over beneath the rap?

genre/joik.text: According to the Sámi, a joik is not a song about someone, but a way of evoking a person, animal or landscape with the voice. Many Sámi had a personal joik of their own. In 1673 Johannes Schefferus was the first to record a joik, but the tradition is centuries old. Missionaries called joiking sinful, and as late as the 1950s it was forbidden in schools. Since Nils-Aslak Valkeapää's record of 1968, the joik has also been heard in pop and jazz.
genre/joik.listen: On this album by Nils-Aslak Valkeapää, a joik for Nils Juhán sounds, surrounded by saxophone and electronic sounds. Listen to how the voice repeats a short motif and varies it slightly. Does the melody have a clear beginning and end, or does it circle round?

genre/jrpg-en-orkestrale-japanse-gamemuz.text: In Japanese role-playing games, the player travels through a world for hours on end. The music therefore often has to repeat without becoming tiresome. Koichi Sugiyama, already experienced in pop and television, wrote music in a classical style for Dragon Quest (1986) and soon had it performed by an orchestra in concerts. Nobuo Uematsu gave Final Fantasy (1987) a melodic character, with influences from progressive rock and Romanticism. For the final battle in Final Fantasy VII (1997), he wrote 'One-Winged Angel', with a choir singing a Latin text. Yasunori Mitsuda composed Chrono Trigger (1995) together with Uematsu. Yoko Shimomura wrote Kingdom Hearts (2002). This music left the screen: orchestral concerts of game music draw full halls worldwide.
genre/jrpg-en-orkestrale-japanse-gamemuz.listen: Notice how a short theme is built as a loop and yet stays varied because the instrument, key or accompaniment keeps changing.

genre/jump-blues.text: Jump blues is the swing of a small band with horns: fast shuffles, boogie-woogie on the piano and a singer who entertains the audience. In the 1940s Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five scored one hit after another with it, such as Caldonia (1945). Rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll grew out of jump blues.
genre/jump-blues.listen: Listen to Caldonia for the small band's shuffle, the saxophone and the shouts of Louis Jordan.
